Without [`--aot`](/bundler/executables#ahead-of-time-compilation), `value as T` is erased, so a test can pass `{ path: "a" } as Entry` for an `Entry` and nobody notices what is missing. Under `--aot`, compiled code relies on `T`, and throws a `TypeError` when the value turns out not to be one.

The rule looks at casts of a value that is written right there: an object or array literal, a string, a number, a boolean, or a `const` that starts with an object literal. It also looks through `as unknown as T` and `as any as T`. For `as never` it uses the type that the place expects. It reports what behaves differently under `--aot`, and nothing else.

{/* Generated by src/codegen/lint-rule-docs.ts. Do not edit this section. */}

## Configure

Off by default. This rule needs types, so turning it on makes `bun lint` type check your code first.

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"bun/aot-cast-lacks-member" = "error" # or "warn"
```

{/* End of the generated section. */}

## Examples

### A number or a boolean is missing

The cast itself doesn't throw. Compiled code keeps a `number`, a `boolean` and a member of a numeric enum without room for `undefined`, so reading the missing member throws, even in a test. Plain JavaScript reads `undefined`.

{/* bad {"count": 2} */}
```ts
interface Entry {
  path: string;
  hasMessages: boolean;
}

function open(entry: Entry) {
  return entry.hasMessages ? entry.path : "";
}

open({ path: "a" } as Entry);
open({ path: "b" } as never);
```

Add the member, or make it optional in the type:

{/* good */}
```ts
interface Entry {
  path: string;
  hasMessages?: boolean;
}

function open(entry: Entry) {
  return entry.hasMessages ? entry.path : "";
}

open({ path: "a" });
```

A missing string, array, object or function reads `undefined` under `--aot` as well, so it isn't reported:

{/* good */}
```ts
interface Reply {
  name: string;
  servers: string[];
}

const reply = { name: "a" } as Reply;
```

### A member of another kind

Code that reads the member as its type throws. A literal inside the literal has to match its type completely, whatever it lacks:

{/* bad {"count": 2} */}
```ts
interface Settings {
  mode: string;
  retry: { times: number; label: string };
}

const wrong = { mode: 1, retry: { times: 1, label: "a" } } as unknown as Settings;
const partial = { mode: "fast", retry: { times: 1 } } as unknown as Settings;
```

### A value that is never of the type

A string, number or boolean is never an object, an array or a function. An object literal is never a string, an array or a function, and it isn't an instance of a class unless it has all its members:

{/* bad {"count": 3} */}
```ts
interface Output {
  text: string;
}

class Timer {
  elapsed = 0;
  stop() {}
}

const output = "done" as unknown as Output;
const lines = { length: 0 } as unknown as string[];
const timer = { elapsed: 1 } as Timer;
```

### Not reported

A cast that can be right, because the value isn't written there:

{/* good */}
```ts
interface Shape {
  kind: string;
}
interface Circle extends Shape {
  radius: number;
}

function radiusOf(shape: Shape) {
  return (shape as Circle).radius;
}

const parsed = JSON.parse("{}") as Circle;
```

An empty object that is filled in afterwards, `null` and `undefined` for a value that is set later, and a literal with a spread or a computed key:

{/* good */}
```ts
interface Circle {
  kind: string;
  radius: number;
}

const circle = {} as Circle;
circle.kind = "circle";
circle.radius = 1;

let selected = null as unknown as Circle;

function withRadius(rest: object) {
  return { kind: "circle", ...rest } as Circle;
}
```

A cast from one primitive type to another converts the value under `--aot`, or throws. `bun check --aot` reports that as `TS100017`.

{/* good */}
```ts
const page = "2" as unknown as number;
```

The rule doesn't compare an object with a type from a declaration file, such as `Date` or a type of a package:

{/* good */}
```ts
const date = { getTime: () => 0 } as unknown as Date;
```
